section.title: Dead to Sin, Alive in Christ
section.sectionRationale: Having declared that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, Paul now answers the obvious objection: shall we then keep on sinning so that grace may increase? His reply is an emphatic no, grounded not in willpower but in union with Christ. We died to sin; we were baptized into His death, buried with Him, and raised with Him to walk in newness of life. Our old self was crucified with Him, so we are to count ourselves dead to sin and alive to God, and refuse to let sin reign, for we are not under law but under grace.
section.thesis: Believers cannot go on living in sin, because in union with Christ they have died to it: joined to His death, burial, and resurrection, their old self was crucified with Him, so they must reckon themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and no longer let sin reign, since they stand not under law but under grace.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the objection answered, we died to sin; baptized into Christ's death and raised to newness of life; our old self crucified with Him; the great reckoning, count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God; and the summons, do not let sin reign, for you are under grace.

units.label: Shall we continue in sin?
units.note: by no means, we died to sin

verses.text: What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?
Certainly not! How can we who died to {{hamartia|sin}} live in it any longer?

units.label: Baptized into His death, raised to new life
units.note: buried with Him, raised to walk in newness of life

verses.text: Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were {{baptizo|baptized}} into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?
We were therefore {{sunthapto|buried with Him}} through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.
For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection.

units.label: Our old self crucified with Him
units.note: the body of sin rendered powerless

verses.text: We know that our {{palaios_anthropos|old self}} was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, that we should no longer be slaves to sin.
For anyone who has died has been freed from sin.

units.label: Count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God

verses.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him.
For we know that since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him.
The death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God.
So you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

units.label: Do not let sin reign
units.note: you are not under law but under grace

verses.text: Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires.

Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness.
For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under {{charis|grace}}.

hamartia.gloss: Sin, a missing of the mark, understood by Paul not merely as separate acts but as a ruling power, almost personified, that enslaves and reigns over people. In Romans 6 sin is the tyrant whose dominion has been broken. To have died to sin is to have been severed from its reign and mastery, so that the believer no longer belongs to it or lives under its rule.

baptizo.gloss: To baptize, to immerse or plunge. Paul says we were baptized into Christ Jesus and into His death. Baptism is the sign and seal of union with Christ, marking the believer's incorporation into His death, burial, and resurrection. The outward washing points to the deeper reality: the believer has been joined to Christ so that His history becomes theirs.

sunthapto.gloss: To bury together with. Paul says we were buried with Christ through baptism into death. Burial confirms that a death has truly occurred; it is the seal on the grave. Believers are so united to Christ that His burial is theirs, the decisive end of the old life, so that they may rise with Him to walk in newness of life.

palaios_anthropos.gloss: The old self or old man, what we were in Adam, the whole person under sin's dominion and condemnation. Paul says this old self was crucified with Christ, put to death in union with Him, so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless. The believer is no longer that person; a decisive break with the old identity has already taken place at the cross.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's undeserved favor and saving power. To be under grace rather than under law is to live in a new realm and under a new King, where sin's dominion is broken. Far from licensing sin, grace is the very reason sin shall not be master, for grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life.

basic.context: Paul has just said that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. That raises a sharp question: if grace grows greater the more we sin, why not sin freely? Paul answers with a resounding no. We died to sin, so how can we still live in it? He explains this through our union with Jesus, pictured in baptism: we were joined to His death, buried with Him, and raised with Him to a new kind of life.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the whole passage as one argument built on union with Christ. Paul reasons from what is already true of believers, we died and were raised with Christ, to how we must now live. The order matters: he does not say try hard to die to sin, but rather know that you have died to sin, then count it true, then live it out. Fact, faith, and then obedience.
basic.originalLanguages: The key words carry the argument. We died to hamartia, sin as a ruling power. We were baptizo, baptized, into Christ's death, and sunthapto, buried with Him. Our palaios anthropos, the old self we were in Adam, was crucified with Him. And now we live under charis, grace, not law, in a new realm where sin cannot reign.
basic.typology: The death and resurrection of Christ, into which the believer is joined, fulfills the pattern of the exodus, where God's people passed through the waters out of bondage into new life. Baptism echoes that passage through water from slavery to freedom. The old self crucified answers the old world drowned in the flood, and new life rising answers the new creation begun in Christ.
basic.christ: Everything here flows from Jesus. His death was a death to sin once for all, and His resurrection is a life lived to God, and both become the believer's own through union with Him. We are baptized into His death, buried with Him, raised with Him. Because He can never die again and death has no dominion over Him, the life we share with Him is secure. Christ is not merely our example but the one in whom we have died and risen.
basic.god: God is the one who raised Christ from the dead through His own glory, and who brings believers from death to life. It is to God that Christ lives, and to God that we are now alive in Christ Jesus. God reigns in grace over those who were once ruled by sin, and He calls them to present themselves to Him as instruments of righteousness.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 5 sets Adam against Christ, the two heads of humanity. Colossians 2 speaks of being buried and raised with Christ in baptism. Galatians 2 declares I have been crucified with Christ. Ephesians 2 says God made us alive together with Christ and raised us up with Him.
basic.oneStory: The Bible tells of humanity enslaved to sin and death since Adam. Here Paul announces the great turning: in Christ, believers have died to that old dominion and risen to new life. The story that ran from bondage in Egypt to the exodus, from exile to return, reaches its fulfillment as sinners are joined to the crucified and risen Lord and set free to walk in newness of life.

context.literary:
Romans 6 answers a question that Paul raised himself, in 3:8 and again in 5:20 and 6:1, and the way he handles it shows his method. He does not reply with a rule or a warning. He replies with a question: 'How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?' To 'live in' sin treats sin as a country one inhabits, and the picture is of a region one has left. Having died, one cannot go on dwelling there.

The paragraph moves in a clean sequence of three verbs of knowing and one of reckoning. 'Aren't you aware,' verse 3, 'we know,' verse 6, 'we know,' verse 9, and then 'count yourselves,' verse 11. Paul argues from what is known to what must be taken as true to what is to be done. The command comes only at verse 12, after eleven verses of statement, and when it comes it is introduced by 'therefore.' This is the pattern of the whole letter: first what God has done, then what follows for the believer's life.

There is also a structure of paired statements. Dying with Christ is matched by rising with Him in verses 4 and 5, and again in verses 8 to 10. Each pair turns on a purpose clause: 'in order that' we may walk in newness of life, verse 4; 'so that' the body of sin might be rendered powerless, verse 6. The list of verbs with the prefix 'with' marks the unity: buried with, united with, crucified with, live with. The passage closes in verse 14 with a promise that echoes 5:21 and prepares for 6:15 to 7:6, where the same objection is raised again and answered with the picture of slavery and marriage.
context.historical:
Baptism was already the rite that marked entry into the Christian community, and for a first hearer it was a vivid act. In the early church believers were baptized by immersion where water allowed, and the going down and coming up gave a ready picture of burial and rising. For a convert out of paganism or Judaism, baptism meant a break with a former world, with its gods, its associations and sometimes its family, and in that setting the language of death and new life did not sound exaggerated.

Paul's opponents in Rome, whether real or imagined, had a point worth taking seriously. A message of free grace had always carried the risk of being heard as licence, and Paul had already met the charge, in Romans 3:8, that he taught people to do evil so that good might result. In a city full of cults that offered ritual purification without moral change, a teaching of forgiveness without transformation would have looked like one more such cult.

Slavery was also a daily reality in Rome, and the second half of the chapter will use it. The hearers knew what it was to be owned, to obey a master, and to be freed or sold. Paul's choice of language about reigning, dominion and being a slave to sin draws on that world. Even the military overtone of verse 13, where the word for 'instruments' can also mean weapons, would be heard in a city whose power rested on its legions. Paul says the believer's body is either a weapon in sin's army or a weapon in God's service, and the choice is between two masters, not between ruling oneself or being ruled.
context.canonical:
The chapter takes its place in a long Biblical story of passing through water. The flood carried Noah and his family through judgment to a new world, and 1 Peter 3:20-21 says that the water of baptism now saves through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The Red Sea took Israel from slavery to freedom, and 1 Corinthians 10:1-2 says that the fathers 'were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.' Romans 6 gathers these into one: baptism into Christ is the new exodus and the new ark.

The idea of death to sin recurs in the apostle's letters. Galatians 2:20 says, 'I have been crucified with Christ.' Colossians 2:12 and 3:1-5 take up the same imagery of burial with Christ and being raised with Him, and ask for the putting to death of earthly desires on that basis. Ephesians 2:4-6 says that God made us alive with Christ and raised us up with Him. Second Corinthians 5:14-15 states that One died for all, therefore all died, and that those who live should no longer live for themselves.

The chapter also looks forward and sideways. Romans 7:1-6 uses the same logic with respect to the law, saying that believers died to the law through the body of Christ. Romans 8:2 says the Spirit of life set us free from the law of sin and death, and Romans 8:11 says the Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to our mortal bodies. First Peter 2:24 says that Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Titus 2:11-12 says the grace of God teaches us to renounce ungodliness, which answers the objection of verse 1 in a single line, and 1 John 3:5-6 says that no one who remains in Him keeps on sinning.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants his readers to see that the gospel of grace is not a loophole. The objection in verse 1 assumes that grace and holiness pull in opposite directions, so that more of one means less of the other. Paul replies that they are not rival options on a scale. They come from the same source, which is the believer's union with Christ. To be in Christ is to have died to sin's reign and to have risen to a new life, and so it makes no sense to ask whether one may go on sinning in order to enjoy more grace.

He also wants to give believers a way to think about themselves. The call in verse 11 is to 'count yourselves,' to take up a settled view of who they are. Behind the command is a conviction that behaviour follows identity. People who believe themselves to be slaves will behave like slaves, and people who see that they have been freed can begin to act like free people. Paul does not deny that sin is still present in the believer, as the later chapters make clear, but he insists that it is no longer the master.

He means the passage to be comforting as well as demanding. Verses 9 and 10 point to the risen Christ over whom death has no more dominion, and the believer shares His life. The newness of life is not a fragile project but a participation in a life that cannot be lost.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage moves from description to prescription in a deliberate order. Verses 2 to 10 describe what is true of every believer: we died to sin, were buried with Christ, were united with Him in His death, and will be united in His resurrection. Verses 11 to 14 then command: count, do not let sin reign, do not present your members to sin, present yourselves to God. The order is the point. The commands rest on the statements, and a person who tries to obey the commands without grasping the statements will be trying to fight a master he has not yet recognised as defeated.

Baptism is mentioned, but the passage is not a manual for the rite. It describes what baptism means, not how to administer it, and it does not settle debates about mode or timing. Equally, the language of 'old self crucified' is not an instruction to hurt or neglect the body. The body is something to be presented to God, verse 13, not rejected.

What the passage does command is a daily habit of mind and a daily presenting of oneself. The verb 'count' is in the present tense, and the command not to let sin reign suggests an ongoing contest. Believers who struggle with sin are not showing that the passage is false. They are being addressed by it, and called to act on what is already true. The call is not to become dead to sin but to reckon that one is.

debates.question: What is the 'baptism into Christ' of verse 3?

views.label: Water baptism as the sign and seal of union
views.case: Most Protestant traditions hold that Paul refers to the rite of baptism, which signifies and seals what the Spirit does by faith. Verse 4 says we were buried 'through baptism,' and the rite's action of going into water and coming out gives the picture. Colossians 2:12 likewise ties burial and rising to baptism and to faith. The water does not itself unite a person to Christ, but it is the appointed sign that sets out the union before the church.

views.label: Spirit baptism, the inward reality
views.case: Some read it as the work of the Spirit by which the believer is placed into Christ's body, as in 1 Corinthians 12:13, with water baptism not primarily in view. They note that Paul's 'baptized into' also appears in 1 Corinthians 10:2, where it describes the exodus and cannot be literal immersion in water of the kind Christians practise.

views.label: The rite as the means by which union is given
views.case: Catholic, Orthodox and some Lutheran traditions teach that baptism is itself a means by which God unites a person to Christ and gives new life, so that the passage describes what happens in the rite. They point to Paul's plain statement that we were buried with Him through baptism, and to Titus 3:5, 'the washing of new birth.'

debates.bearing: All three traditions agree that the thing which matters is union with Christ in His death and resurrection, and that the sign and the reality belong together. Paul's argument works so long as the Roman believers knew that baptism had joined them to Christ, which is how every reading begins.

debates.question: Is the 'we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection' of verse 5 present or future?

views.label: A present, moral resurrection
views.case: The purpose clause in verse 4, 'that we too may walk in newness of life,' shows that Paul is thinking of a present life. The future tense in verses 5 and 8 is then logical, not temporal, meaning that rising with Christ follows necessarily from dying with Him. Verse 11 says believers are already alive to God, and Ephesians 2:5-6 says God has already raised us up with Christ.

views.label: The future bodily resurrection
views.case: Others stress that the future tenses mean what they say. In Paul's letters the believer's bodily resurrection lies ahead, Romans 8:11, and Philippians 3:10-11 speaks of attaining to the resurrection from the dead. The newness of life now is the beginning, but the full union lies at the last day.

views.label: Both, in two stages
views.case: The most common view says Paul holds both: a life already begun by the Spirit, and a resurrection yet to come, with each guaranteed by the other. The present walk in newness of life is the pledge of the future, and the future is the completion of the present.

debates.bearing: Paul's habit is to speak of salvation as already begun and not yet complete. The text sets the present obligation to walk in newness within the larger hope of the body's resurrection, and both depend on Christ's own.

debates.question: What is the 'old self' that was crucified?

views.label: The person I was in Adam
views.case: The phrase palaios anthropos, 'old man,' is read as the whole person under the old order, the person belonging to Adam's age, as Romans 5:12-21 describes. That person was crucified with Christ, and a new person now exists in Him. Colossians 3:9-10 speaks of taking off the old self and putting on the new.

views.label: The sinful nature that remains and must be fought
views.case: Some hold that the old self is the sinful part of the believer that continues to exist and must be put to death daily, in line with Colossians 3:5 and with the struggle Romans 7 describes. On this view believers have two natures.

views.label: A decisive break with ongoing conflict
views.case: Many prefer a middle way, that the old self has been crucified in the sense that its rule is broken, while the flesh remains and wages war against the Spirit, Galatians 5:17. The believer has one new identity in Christ and still battles the remnants of the old life.

debates.bearing: The tense of verse 6 is aorist, and the result clause speaks of sin's body being rendered powerless, not annihilated. That favours the third view: the old ruler is deposed, and the fight is about living under the new one.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to see is the Greek idiom of verse 2, me genoito, literally 'may it not be,' which the BSB renders 'Certainly not!' Paul uses it repeatedly in Romans, for instance in 3:4, 3:6 and 3:31, as the strongest possible rejection of an objection. The same phrase will return in 6:15, where the question is asked again in a slightly different form.

Notice the tense of the verb in verse 2, 'we died to sin.' It is the aorist apethanomen, which looks at the death as one finished event. Sin is hamartia, and Paul uses it in this chapter mostly in the singular, as a power and not only as individual acts. The believer has not stopped committing sins in some perfect way. Paul says that he has died to a master.

Baptizo in verse 3 is passive, 'were baptized,' and the preposition is eis, 'into.' To be baptized into Christ is to be placed within Him, and the same phrase in 1 Corinthians 10:2 says the fathers were baptized 'into Moses,' meaning brought under his leadership and into the redemption he mediated. In Galatians 3:27 the same idea leads to being 'clothed' with Christ.

There is a family of compounds with the prefix syn, 'with,' that holds the passage together. Verse 4 has sunthapto, 'buried with,' verse 5 has symphytoi, which is usually translated 'united' and literally pictures things grown together, as a graft or a planting. Verse 6 has synestaurothe, 'crucified with,' and verse 8 has syzesomen, 'we will live with.' The believer's story is told in the grammar of togetherness.

The verb in verse 6, katargeo, 'rendered powerless,' is a word that means to make inoperative or to put out of action. It does not mean to destroy. Paul uses it in 3:31 for the law, which faith does not 'nullify,' and in 7:2 and 7:6 for being released from the law. The body of sin is not annihilated but disabled, and the same verb in the same letter shows that a thing can be made ineffective without ceasing to exist.

Verse 7 contains a legal surprise. 'Freed' translates dedikaiotai, a form of dikaioo, the verb 'justify' that dominates chapters 3 to 5. The verse says, in effect, that the one who has died has been justified from sin. The legal principle is that death settles a claim, and Paul applies it to the believer's death with Christ. In Romans 7:1-3 he uses the same rule in the case of marriage.

In verse 10 the phrase 'once for all' is ephapax, the word that Hebrews uses repeatedly for the sacrifice of Christ, Hebrews 7:27 and 10:10. In verse 9 'dominion' is kyrieuei, from kyrios, 'lord.' Death used to be lord, and no longer is. In verse 14 the same root appears when Paul says sin 'shall not be your master,' kyrieusei.

In verse 11 the key word is logizesthe, 'count,' the same verb that dominated chapter 4, where righteousness was 'credited.' Paul's command is to keep an honest ledger: to reckon as true what God has already counted true. It is in the present tense, a continuing practice.

In verse 13 the verb 'present' is paristemi, and Paul sets a present imperative negatively, 'do not keep presenting,' against an aorist imperative positively, 'present yourselves once for all.' The first speaks of stopping a habit, and the second of a decisive act of dedication. The Greek noun hopla, rendered 'instruments,' can also mean weapons, which gives the line a military edge. Finally, in verse 14 'under grace' is hypo charin. The preposition hypo means 'under the authority of,' so that the contrast is between two regimes, two sovereigns.

typology.type: The crossing of the Red Sea, Exodus 14:21-22
typology.fulfillment: Israel passed through the sea with walls of water on either side, and the Egyptians who pursued them were gone by morning, Exodus 14:30-31. Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:1-2 calls this a baptism into Moses. In Romans 6 it is the pattern for a deeper passage: through the water of death with Christ, out of the slavery of sin into freedom. The escalation is that the Lord brings the believer through His own death, not just alongside it. The type falls short because Israel came up on the far shore and soon grumbled for Egypt again, while the believer is raised into a life that has the Spirit as its power.

The flood was a judgment that swept away an old world while the ark carried a few through to a new one, 1 Peter 3:20-21. Peter says that baptism corresponds to the water of the flood, not as the removal of dirt but as the pledge of a clear conscience through the resurrection of Jesus. In Romans 6 the old self is judged and left behind, and the believer comes up into a renewed existence. The type falls short because Noah's family carried the same sinful nature into the new world, Genesis 8:21, while those in Christ are given a new heart.

typology.type: Adam as a pattern of the One to come, Romans 5:14
typology.fulfillment: Paul says outright that Adam is a pattern of Christ, in the sense that each is a head whose act determines the standing of those who belong to him. Romans 6 applies this. Those in Adam were under sin and death, and those in Christ have died and risen with Him. The escalation is that Christ's act is greater than Adam's, Romans 5:15-17. The type falls short because Adam's act brought condemnation while Christ's brings life, and the parallel is one of contrast as much as of likeness.

The rite of circumcision marked a cutting away of flesh as a sign of belonging to God's covenant, Genesis 17:10-11. The prophets asked for a circumcised heart, Deuteronomy 30:6, and Colossians 2:11-12 links the putting off of the sinful nature to the circumcision done by Christ and to burial and resurrection in baptism. The passage in Romans 6 shows the same movement of cutting off the old and entering the new. The type falls short because the outward rite could be performed on someone whose heart was untouched, while the inward cutting is the work of Christ.

study.christ:
The chapter is a statement about what happened to Jesus and what that means for those who belong to Him. Its central claim is that the believer's history has been folded into Christ's. When Paul says 'we were baptized into His death,' he means more than that the death of Christ was an example, or that it paid for sins we would then leave behind. He means that those who are in Christ were included in that death. Second Corinthians 5:14 states it plainly: One died for all, therefore all died. In the cross, the sin-bound self was dealt with in His body.

Verse 10 says He 'died to sin once for all.' That does not mean Christ ever had a sinful past to leave, since Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way yet without sin. It means that He entered fully into the domain where sin and death reign, bore its cost, and then passed out of its reach for good. Sin had a claim on Him only as the bearer of ours, and when that debt was paid the claim lapsed. The life He now lives, 'He lives to God,' is a life with no further relation to sin's rule, and the believer who has died with Him shares that new existence.

Verse 9 says that death no longer has dominion over Him. That echoes the resurrection testimony of the Gospels and of Revelation 1:18, where the risen Lord says He was dead and is alive forever and holds the keys of death and of Hades. The grounds for the believer's confidence in the struggle are therefore not in himself but in the one who has defeated the master. Hebrews 2:14-15 says that through death He destroyed the one who holds the power of death and freed those held in slavery by the fear of it.

The passage also presents Christ as the second head of humanity. Having set Adam beside Him in 5:12-21, Paul shows in chapter 6 what it means to be in the second Adam: a participation that affects not just the verdict but the person. This is why union with Christ is the root of both justification and sanctification. The one in whom we are counted righteous is the one in whom we died to sin and in whom we now live. Paul can say in Galatians 2:20 that Christ lives in him, and in Romans 8:11 that the same Spirit who raised Christ will give life to mortal bodies.

Finally, Christ is the pattern as well as the ground. The shape of the believer's life, going down into death to self and rising to live for God, follows His own. Philippians 3:10 speaks of knowing the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death. We have to be careful, though, not to flatten the difference: His death was unique and substitutionary, and ours is a sharing in His. The passage does not need allegory to be rich. Its links are the explicit ones the New Testament draws between baptism, burial, cross and resurrection.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the one who acts decisively and the one who calls His people to live in response. The most important verb is passive: we 'were baptized,' we 'were buried,' our old self 'was crucified.' All of these are things done to us by God in Christ. The whole structure of the Christian life rests on God's act and not on ours, and so the commands of verses 11 to 13 never turn into a program of self-rescue.

God is the God of resurrection. Verse 4 says Christ was raised 'through the glory of the Father,' a phrase that describes the whole weight of the Father's majesty and power acting in the event. The same God who made the world and raised the dead is at work in the believer's new life, Romans 8:11. This is why Paul can speak of walking in newness of life without fear of failing in his own strength. The power at work is God's.

The passage also shows God as a sovereign who frees and claims. Verse 14 says sin shall not be your master because you are under grace, which means that the believer has changed rulers. God's grace is described not as a mood but as a reign, a regime with its own authority. The grace that rules is not weaker than the law. It is stronger, since it can do what the law could not, Romans 8:3. And a grace that reigns is a grace that makes subjects holy.

God's holiness is plain throughout. He does not treat sin as a small thing. The cross required a death, and the believer's union with Christ means that sin's claim is broken by dying and not by being ignored. Paul's refusal of the idea that grace makes room for sin, 'Certainly not!', is a statement of God's character. A God who is holy could not give a grace that leaves His people in the grip of what He hates, and Titus 2:11-12 says that this grace trains us to renounce ungodliness.

God is also generous. The invitation to present ourselves to Him in verse 13 comes after the statement that we have been brought from death to life. He does not demand service from the dead. He raises them, and then asks that the life be given back to Him. Romans 12:1 makes the same appeal: in view of God's mercy, offer your bodies as living sacrifices.

For worship, the chapter produces a particular kind of sobriety and joy. The sobriety comes from recognising that the cross was the end of one life, and the joy from knowing it is the beginning of another. Every baptism and every Lord's Supper recalls it, and every day of obedience is an act of gratitude to the God who has made it possible.

crossReferences.note: The statements that raise the question of Romans 6:1: where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life. Paul answers the objection by showing that grace does reign, and that its reign leads to righteousness, not to more sin.

Christ's circumcision, burial and resurrection with faith in the power of God. It gives a parallel to verse 4, adds the picture of circumcision as a putting off of the sinful nature, and shows that Paul taught the same union to a church he had never visited.

Paul's personal statement, 'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.' It says in the first person what Romans 6 says of all believers, and it shows that union with Christ was not a doctrine for others only but his own lived reality, held by faith in the Son who loved him.

God made us alive with Christ, raised us up and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms. It states the resurrection side of Romans 6:4 and 6:5 as an accomplished event, and traces it to God's great love and mercy, not to our effort.

Believers died to the law through the body of Christ, in order to belong to Him who was raised, and to bear fruit to God. It uses the logic of Romans 6:7 on a second front, and shows that union with Christ has a purpose: fruitfulness, not just freedom.

Since you have been raised with Christ, set your minds on things above, and put to death what is earthly. It shows how Paul turns the indicative into the imperative in another letter, and uses the same order as Romans 6:11 to 13: first what is true, then what to do.

The fathers were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. It gives an Old Testament pattern for the idea of being baptized into someone, and links the exodus with the baptism language of Romans 6:3 and 6:4.

The water of the flood corresponds to baptism, which saves through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, as the pledge of a clear conscience toward God. It shows another early reading of baptism as passage through judgment into new life, and guards against thinking the water cleans by itself.

The grace of God that brings salvation also instructs us to renounce ungodliness and live upright lives. It answers the objection of Romans 6:1 in a sentence and shows that Paul's reply there was not a special pleading but a standard part of his teaching.

One died for all, therefore all died, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves. It sets out the principle of representation that lies under Romans 6:3 to 7, and gives the purpose of the death as a new orientation of life toward Christ.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's opening chapters describe a human race that went into sin under a single head and has lived under its reign ever since. Genesis 3 brought death, and Genesis 5 repeats the refrain 'and he died.' The rest of the Old Testament tells of attempts to break the rule: the law was given, the sacrifices were offered, prophets called for repentance, and the people went into exile and returned. None of it ended the reign. Paul will say in Romans 8:3 that the law itself could not, since it was weakened by the flesh.

Romans 6 is the place where the reign is broken. Not by a new effort, but by a death. Jesus went into the domain of sin and death on behalf of His people and came out the other side, and those who belong to Him went with Him. This is the second exodus, the real one. Israel's first exodus rescued a people from Pharaoh, and this one rescues a people from sin and from the death that sin brings. The Red Sea is crossed in baptism, the flood is survived, and a new humanity stands on the far shore.

The chapter also sits where the story turns toward the life of the Spirit. Once death and sin have lost their hold, the question is what to do with the freedom, and chapters 6 to 8 answer it: serve God as slaves of righteousness, die to the law's condemnation, and walk by the Spirit. The story does not stop at forgiveness. It reaches for transformation, and it does so on the basis of union.

The end of the Bible shows where this leads. In Revelation 21:4 death will be no more, and in Revelation 22:3 there will be no more curse. The 'newness of life' of Romans 6:4 is the first fruit of a new creation, and the resurrection which Paul says we will certainly share, verse 5, completes it. What Adam lost and Christ won, the whole creation will receive when the sons of God are revealed, Romans 8:19-23.

quiz.q: How does Paul answer the objection, shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?

options.text: Certainly not, because we died to sin and cannot live in it any longer.
options.note: Paul grounds his no in the believer's death to sin in union with Christ.

options.text: We may sin a little, since grace covers it anyway.
options.note: This is the very error Paul rejects; grace does not license sin.

options.text: We should sin so that grace can be displayed more fully.
options.note: Paul calls this unthinkable; it contradicts our death to sin.

options.text: Sin is no longer a real problem for believers.
options.note: There is real truth that sin's reign is broken, yet Paul still says do not let sin reign, so it must be resisted.

quiz.q: What does baptism into Christ signify, according to Paul?

options.text: Union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection.
options.note: We were baptized into His death, buried with Him, and raised to new life.

options.text: Only a public ceremony with no deeper meaning.
options.note: Baptism is indeed an outward sign, but it points to the deeper reality of union with Christ, so this understates its meaning.

options.text: A guarantee of salvation apart from faith in Christ.
options.note: The sign points to union with Christ received by faith, not the rite working of itself.

options.text: The moment a person earns God's favor by obedience.
options.note: Union with Christ is by grace, not earned by the act.

quiz.q: What happened to the old self, according to verse 6?

options.text: It was crucified with Christ so the body of sin might be rendered powerless.
options.note: The old man in Adam was put to death in union with Christ.

options.text: It was gradually improved until it became good.
options.note: There is real growth in holiness, but Paul speaks of a decisive crucifixion of the old self, not mere gradual improvement.

options.text: It remains fully in charge of the believer's life.
options.note: The old self was crucified so we are no longer slaves to sin.

options.text: It was left untouched by the work of Christ.
options.note: It was crucified with Him; the break is real and decisive.

quiz.q: What does Paul command believers to do in verse 11?

options.text: Count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
options.note: Faith reckons true what God has accomplished in Christ.

options.text: Try by willpower to make yourselves die to sin.
options.note: The believer must actively respond, but reckons a death already accomplished in Christ rather than achieving it by willpower.

options.text: Wait passively until sin stops troubling you.
options.note: Paul calls for active reckoning and then active obedience.

options.text: Assume sin no longer exists in your life at all.
options.note: Sin remains to be resisted; that is why Paul says do not let it reign.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say sin shall not be your master?

options.text: Because you are not under law but under grace.
options.note: Grace is a new reign in which sin's dominion is broken.

options.text: Because believers are now strong enough to defeat sin alone.
options.note: Believers do resist sin, but the ground is grace and union with Christ, not their own strength.

options.text: Because the law has finally made us righteous.
options.note: It is grace, not law, that frees from sin's dominion.

options.text: Because sin was never really a serious threat.
options.note: Sin is a real tyrant whose reign is broken only in Christ.

questions: Paul says believers have died to sin. How does knowing that your union with Christ is an accomplished fact change the way you fight temptation?
Baptism pictures being buried and raised with Christ. What would it mean for you to live today as someone who has truly been brought from death to life?
Paul commands us to count ourselves dead to sin and alive to God. Where do you need to reckon as true what God has already made true of you in Christ?
We are told not to present the parts of our body to sin but to God as instruments of righteousness. What specific part of your life needs to be presented to God this week?
Sin shall not be your master because you are under grace. How does living under grace, rather than under law, actually free you to pursue holiness?

translationNotes.note: How can we who died to sin renders an aorist that points to a decisive past event, not a gradual process; the believer has already died to sin's dominion in union with Christ.
Buried with Him renders synthapto, buried together with; baptism into death signifies real union with Christ's burial, sealing the end of the old life before rising to newness of life.

Count yourselves renders a word meaning reckon or consider as an accounting term; it calls for faith to treat as true the death and life already accomplished in Christ, not to pretend or to strive to make it so.
